title: The U.S. Oil Sector's Role in Restraining Prices - Liberty Street Economics
gist: NY Fed's Thomas Klitgaard argues the U.S. oil sector kept the 2026 Middle East supply shock (global output down 12 mb/d in March) from producing record prices: shale-driven oversupply (U.S. output 8 to 21 mb/d over 2010-2025) had global inventories building ~4 mb/d before the conflict, and U.S. SPR (1 mb/d) and commercial (0.7 mb/d) drawdowns covered about half the Q2 global gap. U.S. stocks stopped falling in July, so the ongoing ~3 mb/d global draw now falls on other countries, notably China; outcomes hinge on whether Middle East output recovers or demand must be destroyed.

themes.theme: US shale as shock absorber in the 2026 Middle East supply shock

insights.claim: The Middle East conflict that began in early 2026 caused an unprecedented drop in global petroleum supply, yet oil prices rose but did not reach unprecedented levels, largely because of the U.S. oil sector.
insights.speaker: Thomas Klitgaard
insights.so_what: Price response to supply shocks is now dampened by US supply and inventory buffers; size geopolitical oil-spike trades accordingly.
insights.quote: oil prices jumped—but not to unprecedentedly high levels

insights.claim: U.S. commercial and government (SPR) inventory drawdowns filled roughly half of the global supply-demand gap in Q2 2026, with the SPR releasing about 1 mb/d and commercial stocks falling about 0.7 mb/d.
insights.speaker: Thomas Klitgaard
insights.so_what: US stockpiles were the main marginal supplier during the shock; their exhaustion removes a key price cushion.
insights.quote: the SPR releasing crude oil at the rate of 1 mb/d in the second quarter and commercial inventories falling at a 0.7 mb/d rate

insights.claim: U.S. net petroleum exports rose 2.5 mb/d in Q2 2026 (exports up 2 mb/d, imports down 0.5 mb/d) as domestic inventory drawdowns made more oil available to the rest of the world.
insights.speaker: Thomas Klitgaard
insights.so_what: Watch US net export data as a real-time gauge of how much buffer the US is supplying to global markets.

insights.so_what: The US buffer is spent; continued global deficits must be met elsewhere, raising risk of tighter prices.

insights.so_what: China's depleted stocks imply future restocking demand once the conflict eases, supporting prices on the way down.

insights.speaker: Thomas Klitgaard

insights.claim: U.S. output of crude and other liquid fuels rose from 8 mb/d in 2010 to 21 mb/d in 2025, accounting for about 70% of the 19 mb/d rise in global production over that period, driven by fracking.
insights.speaker: Thomas Klitgaard
insights.so_what: US shale is the dominant marginal source of global supply growth, making US drilling a key price determinant.

insights.speaker: Thomas Klitgaard
insights.so_what: US macro sensitivity to oil shocks has structurally fallen since the shift to net exporter.

insights.claim: The 2015 repeal of a 1975 law largely banning crude exports sustained the production surge, because Permian Basin output exceeded Gulf refinery capacity and exports relieved the bottleneck.
insights.speaker: Thomas Klitgaard
insights.so_what: Policy access to export markets is what kept US shale investment growing; reversals would cap supply.

insights.speaker: Thomas Klitgaard
insights.so_what: The US is now a net petroleum exporter, so higher oil prices are a terms-of-trade gain rather than a pure drag.
